I can't reproduce the full guide verbatim, but here's a concise summary of the setup steps.

**Prerequisites:** Node.js 24 or later. Ascribe supports macOS (Apple silicon), Linux (x64 and arm64), and Windows (x64).

**1. Install the CLI** as a dev dependency with npm or pnpm, then confirm the `ascribe` binary runs. The latest release is 0.2.0. Optionally, install the Ascribe VS Code extension for live checking, completion, and previews.

**2. Create `ascribe.toml`** in the project root. The minimal file only declares the spec version `0.1`. You can also declare dimensions (such as a package-manager choice), phrases (reusable values like a product name and version), and a consumer site URL. Add the `.ascribe/` output directory to `.gitignore`.

**3. Write a first page** in `docs/`. The guide's example uses frontmatter with a `title`, a tip callout, variant blocks that show different content per package manager, a steps list, and a link to another page by filename. Ascribe generates the URL.

**4. Check the project.** Running the check command reports problems such as a link to a missing file, each with a diagnostic code. It exits with status 1 on errors, and `--deny-warnings` also fails on warnings. Create the missing page and check again.

**5. Build.** The build writes three outputs to `.ascribe/build/<build>/`: `site/` (for Astro), `plain/` (plain Markdown), and `json/` (resolved pages as JSON).

**6. Format.** The format command normalizes directive syntax. Its check mode reports needed changes without modifying files, which suits CI.

**7. Publish with Astro.** In an Astro project, install `@ascribed/astro`, register the integration in `astro.config.mjs` with your site URL and the `site` build, then define a content collection, a route, and a layout. The Astro guide walks through these.

**8. Run checks in CI.** Use a pull-request workflow on Node 24 that installs dependencies, runs the check with `--deny-warnings`, and runs the format check.

**9. AI agents (not yet released, available on main).** Running the `agents sync` command writes an `AGENTS.md` file with your project's rules and a skill that helps an agent check its own edits.

**Further reading:** the directive reference, the `ascribe.toml` reference, the command reference, the diagnostics reference, the editing guide, the Astro guide, and the agents guide, all on ascribed-dev.com.

Getting started
Install Ascribe, write a first page, check it, build it, and publish it with Astro.

For AI agents: the documentation index is at [/llms.txt] llms.txt, and this page is available as [/getting-started.md] Markdown.

Ascribe is documentation written as code: Markdown with a small set of directives for the structure documentation needs (notes, procedures, alternatives by platform or product, availability, includes), checked like code, and built into a website, plain Markdown, and JSON. This guide sets up a project, writes a first page, and publishes it with Astro.

You need [https://nodejs.org] Node.js 24 or later. Ascribe runs on macOS on Apple silicon, Linux (x64 and arm64, with glibc 2.28 or later (2.39 for 0.1.1 and earlier), which includes the build images of Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare Pages, and AWS Amplify), and Windows (x64).

Install the command

In your project’s directory:

npm install --save-dev @ascribed/cli
npx ascribe --version

pnpm add --save-dev @ascribed/cli
pnpm exec ascribe --version

@ascribed/cli installs the ascribe binary for your platform, and pins its version for everyone who works on the project, and for CI. The latest release is 0.2.0. If ascribe can’t find the binary, your package manager left out optional dependencies; reinstall with them enabled.

To try what’s on main before it’s released, install @ascribed/cli@next and @ascribed/astro@next instead: a build published every night, with no promise of stability.

Install the editor

Install the Ascribe extension for VS Code from the Marketplace:

code --install-extension Ascribe.ascribe-vscode

It checks your pages as you type, completes directives, [/reference/directives/#phrases] phrases, and links, and previews pages as the site shows them. It uses the project’s ascribe when there is one. See [/guides/editor/] Editing.

Ascribe (in main, not yet released)

After you install it, its walkthrough, Get Started with Ascribe, shows the preview, the actions bar that writes directives for you, and the Ascribe sidebar. It’s under Help → Welcome whenever you want it again.

Create ascribe.toml

ascribe.toml is the [/reference/content-model/] content model: the project’s schema. It marks the project root, and the smallest one is a single line:

spec = "0.1"

With nothing else declared, pages live in docs/, output goes to .ascribe/build/, every page needs a title, and there’s one build, site. A more useful start declares a [/reference/content-model/#6-dimensionsname] dimension your content varies by, and a few phrases:

spec = "0.1"

[dimensions.pm]
label = "Package manager"
values = ["npm", "pnpm", "yarn"]

[phrases]
product = "Quill"
version = "3.4.1"

[consumer]
site = "https://docs.example.com"

The [/reference/content-model/] ascribe.toml reference covers every section: content types and their frontmatter, availability, features, the glossary, project widgets, and builds.

Add the output directory to .gitignore:

.ascribe/

Write a page

Create docs/install.md:

---
title: Install Quill
---

@note {type=tip}: {product} {version} needs Node.js 22 or later.

## Install the package

@variant {pm=npm}:
```sh
npm install quill
```
@variant {pm=pnpm}:
```sh
pnpm add quill
```
@variant {pm=yarn}:
```sh
yarn add quill
```
@end

## Set it up

@steps
1. Create `quill.yaml`.
2. Run `quill init`.

Next, [configure it](configure.md).

@note is a callout; {type=tip} is its attribute.

@variant marks alternatives by package manager. The site shows them as tabs, and a build can keep just one.

{product} and {version} are phrases from ascribe.toml.

@steps marks the list as a procedure.

The link points at a file, configure.md. Ascribe writes the URL.

The [/reference/directives/] directive reference describes every directive and inline construct.

Check it

npx ascribe check

The link to configure.md is reported, since that page doesn’t exist yet:

[ASC036] Error: `configure.md` doesn't exist
    ╭─[ docs/install.md:29:22 ]
    │
 29 │ Next, [configure it](configure.md).
    │                      ──────┬─────
    │                            ╰─────── link-target-missing
────╯
checked 1 file: 1 error, 0 warnings

Every diagnostic has a code, and the [/reference/diagnostics/] diagnostics reference says how to fix each. ascribe check exits with 1 when there are errors, so it can gate CI; add --deny-warnings to fail on warnings too. Create docs/configure.md with a title, and check again.

Build it

npx ascribe build

Each build writes three outputs to .ascribe/build/<build>/:

site/: Markdown with web components, for Astro;

plain/: plain Markdown with everything resolved, for search indexes and LLMs;

json/: the resolved pages as JSON, for your own tools.

See the [/reference/cli/#cli-build] command reference.

Format it

npx ascribe fmt

rewrites directives and attribute blocks into their canonical spelling, and changes nothing else. ascribe fmt --check reports what would change, for CI.

Publish it with Astro

In an [https://astro.build] Astro project (npm create astro@latest makes one), with ascribe.toml beside astro.config.mjs:

Install the integration:

npm install @ascribed/astro

Add it to astro.config.mjs:

// astro.config.mjs
import { defineConfig } from "astro/config";
import ascribe from "@ascribed/astro";

export default defineConfig({
  site: "https://docs.example.com",
  integrations: [ascribe({ build: "site" })],
});

Define the content collection, a route, and a layout that loads the elements. [/guides/astro/] Astro walks through each file.

Check it in CI

Run the same command the editor runs:

# .github/workflows/docs.yml
name: Docs
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx ascribe check --deny-warnings
      - run: npx ascribe fmt --check

Work with an AI agent

Ascribe (in main, not yet released)

If you write with an AI coding agent, such as Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, or Codex, give it your project’s rules:

Ascribe (in main, not yet released)

npx ascribe agents sync

pnpm exec ascribe agents sync

Ascribe (in main, not yet released)

That writes AGENTS.md, with your page types, phrases, and the check to run after each edit, and a skill that teaches the agent to check and fix its own work. Most agents read both on their own. [/guides/agents/] Agents covers the rest: the commands an agent uses, prompts you hand it, the MCP server, and hooks that check each edit.

Next

[/reference/directives/] Directive reference: the language.

[/reference/content-model/] ascribe.toml reference: the content model.

[/reference/cli/] Command reference: check, build, fmt, and lsp.

[/reference/diagnostics/] Diagnostics: every problem Ascribe reports, and its fix.

[/guides/editor/] Editing: the VS Code extension.

[/guides/astro/] Astro: publishing a site.

Ascribe (in main, not yet released)

[/guides/agents/] Agents: working with an AI coding agent.

# Astro

`@ascribed/astro` publishes an Ascribe project as an [Astro](https://astro.build) site. It runs `ascribe build --emit site` before Astro loads content, gives you a content collection of the built pages with a schema generated from `ascribe.toml`, applies heading ids and image attributes in Astro's own Markdown pipeline (so Astro's table of contents and image processing still work), loads the element library, and serves the files pages link to. In `astro dev`, it rebuilds as you edit.

It supports Astro 7.3.5 and later 7.x releases.

## Set up a site

These steps add Ascribe to an Astro project. [`examples/astro-site`](https://github.com/ascribed-dev/ascribe/tree/main/examples/astro-site) is a complete site built this way.

### 1\. Install

**npm**

```sh
npm install @ascribed/astro
```

**pnpm**

```sh
pnpm add @ascribed/astro
```

It brings `@ascribed/cli`, the `ascribe` command for your platform, and `@ascribed/elements`. Astro's image processing also needs `sharp` (`npm install sharp`) if your project doesn't have it.

```toml
base-path = "/docs/"

```

Required. | | `project` | The directory holding `ascribe.toml`, relative to the Astro root. By default, the root. | | `binary` | The `ascribe` binary to run, relative to the Astro root. By default, `false`, though `review` turns them on in `astro dev`. | | `review` (Available: Ascribe (GA, 0.2.0+)) | [Review in the site preview](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/astro/#review-in-the-site-preview): the **Ascribe review** app in `astro dev`'s toolbar. `false` leaves it out. Changes are batched, and builds run one at a time. - After a successful rebuild, Astro reloads the collection and the page. - After a failed one, the diagnostics are in Astro's terminal, and pages answer with HTTP 503 until a save builds cleanly again, so you never see a stale page. - A change to `[project] output-dir` needs a restart of `astro dev`, and says so. - Available: Ascribe (GA, 0.2.0+) It writes where it's running (`url` and `build`) to `.ascribe/dev.json` in the project, for the editor's [Open Site Preview](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/editor/#site-preview), and removes the file when it stops. ## Publish for AI agents Available: Ascribe (in main, not yet released) An AI agent reading your docs does better with Markdown than with HTML, and with an index to choose pages from. Turn on the outputs for agents in `ascribe.toml`'s `[consumer]`, beside `site`, and each build publishes them with the site, as the [Web Documentation Delivery Spec](https://agentdocsspec.com/spec/web/) lays them out: ```toml # llms.txt, a Markdown version of each page, and a pointer to the index on # each: what agents read. `@ascribed/astro` publishes them with the site. agents = true ``` - **`llms.txt`** at the base path: every page, by folder, as its title, a link to its Markdown, and its description (the field its type marks `role = "description"`). Past 50,000 characters it's split into one `llms.txt` per folder, which the root file links to. - **Each page's Markdown** at its URL with `.md`: `/docs/guides/setup` is also `/docs/guides/setup.md`. - **A pointer** at the top of each page to both, which the elements' stylesheet hides from sight but not from an agent reading the page. `site` is required, because everything an agent reads links by absolute URL. The integration builds the plain output too, copies it into the built site, and serves it in `astro dev`. The [`ascribe.toml` reference](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/content-model/#15-consumer) says how `llms.txt` is put together. `ascribe check` then adds two pieces of advice: a page whose description is too long for its line in `llms.txt`, and an `llms.txt` that's still too long when split. Write each page's `description` as one sentence saying what the page is for; it's what an agent picks a page by. ### What your host does The files are static, so any host serves them. A few things the spec asks are the server's, not the build's: - **The `.md` files' type.** Serve them as `text/markdown; charset=utf-8`, and `llms.txt` as `text/plain; charset=utf-8`, as `astro dev` does. Check what your host sends (`curl -I` a page's `.md`), and set the header in its configuration if it's something else. - **Content negotiation.** An agent may ask for a page with `Accept: text/markdown`; answering it with the page's `.md` needs a rule on the server, such as an edge function or middleware that rewrites to `<path>.md` when that header asks for Markdown. Without it, agents still find the `.md` URLs through `llms.txt` and the pointer. On Netlify, an edge function does it: this site's is [`markdown.ts`](https://github.com/ascribed-dev/ascribe/blob/main/site/netlify/edge-functions/markdown.ts). - **Status codes and caching.** A missing page should answer 404, not 200 with a page saying so, and the `.md` files and `llms.txt` should be cached no longer than the pages. - **Bot protection.** A rule that challenges unfamiliar clients blocks agents too; let them read `llms.txt` and the `.md` files. ## Permalinks Available: Ascribe (in main, not yet released) A heading marked as a [permalink](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/directives/#permalinks), `@id {permalink=true}: weave-config`, gets an address of its own, `go/weave-config` under the base path, which sends the reader to the heading wherever it is now. A page with `permalink: options` in its frontmatter gets `go/options`, which leads to the top of the page. Link to that address from outside the docs, such as from your product's interface or its error messages, and the link keeps working when the page moves. The integration adds the route itself, from the list each build writes (`_ascribe/permalinks.json` in the site output, [output-layout contract §1.2](https://ascribed-dev.com/contracts/output-layout/#12-the-permalinks-list)). Each address is a small page that: - forwards at once with a `<meta http-equiv="refresh">`, without a script, keeping a heading's anchor; - with a script, first takes the reader's choices from the address's parameters ([Linking from a product](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/astro/#linking-from-a-product)); - links to the same place, for a browser that doesn't follow; - is marked `noindex`, with a canonical link to where it leads, so search engines list the page and not the address. So it works on any static host, in `astro build` and in `astro dev`, where a permalink you add or remove is served on the next rebuild, with no restart. The addresses end the way the site's routes do (`trailing-slash`), and aren't pages of the collection, `llms.txt`, or the Markdown for agents. [`permalink-path`](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/content-model/#15-consumer) moves them, as a path from the site's root, such as `"/go/"` when the docs move under `/docs/` but the addresses your product prints shouldn't. It must be under Astro's `base`, since that's all an Astro site serves; the integration fails the build when it isn't. **With another generator,** read `_ascribe/permalinks.json` from the build's site output and publish a page like these at `path` and each name, forwarding to `route`, and `#` and `fragment` for a heading. For the parameters, its script calls `@ascribed/elements`' `choose` for each one that names a [dimension](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/content-model/#6-dimensionsname) in the list's `dimensions` with one of its values, then forwards. A host's redirect rules can do the same as the page without its script, but a redirect drops nothing only if the host keeps the anchor. ### Linking from a product A product links to a permalink's address: the site, the permalinks' path, and the name, ending the way the site's routes do. It can add what it knows about its reader, as parameters named for the content model's [dimensions](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/content-model/#6-dimensionsname): ```ts // The docs' permalinks, as `[consumer]` publishes them. const permalinks = "https://docs.example.com/docs/go/"; function docsLink(name: string, reader: Record<string, string> = {}): string { const url = new URL(name, permalinks); for (const [dimension, value] of Object.entries(reader)) url.searchParams.set(dimension, value); return url.href; } // https://docs.example.com/docs/go/weave-config?pm=pnpm docsLink("weave-config", { pm: "pnpm" }); ``` - **A parameter that names a dimension, with one of its values,** sets the reader's choice for that dimension, as if they'd picked the tab: the section opens with the `pnpm` tab showing, and the choice holds on the pages they read next. - **Anything else is ignored:** a name that isn't a dimension, or a value the dimension doesn't have. Send what the product knows, without checking what the docs accept; a link with only unknown parameters works as one with none. - **The choice needs a script and the browser's storage.** With scripts off, the address forwards to the section with the tabs as they were; with storage blocked, the choice doesn't reach the next page. - **A version isn't a parameter yet.** `self-managed=3.4` is ignored like any unknown one. ### Checking a product's links A product that links to the docs can check, in its own CI, that every name it links to is still a permalink there, without building or even having the docs. The docs commit their list of permalinks, `ascribe.permalinks`, which `ascribe permalinks sync` writes beside `ascribe.toml` ([The permalinks list](https://ascribed-dev.com/contracts/permalinks-list/)). Then `ascribe check` in the docs warns when a permalink is removed, and the product checks its names against a copy of the list: ```yaml # .github/workflows/docs-links.yml, in the product's repository name: Docs links on: [pull_request] jobs: docs-links: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 # The docs' list, from their repository; or keep a copy in this one. - run: curl -fsSL -o docs.permalinks https://raw.githubusercontent.com/example/docs/main/ascribe.permalinks - run: npx @ascribed/cli permalinks verify --list docs.permalinks --from docs-links.txt ``` `docs-links.txt` lists the names the product links to, one on each line. [`ascribe permalinks verify`](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/cli/#cli-permalinks-verify) exits with 1, naming each name the list doesn't have, and each the docs retired, with the reason they gave, so a link to a section the docs removed, or never had, fails the product's pull request rather than reaching its users. An alias passes, as the permalink it leads to does. In the docs, `ascribe check` reports a list that's behind the content (`permalinks-list-behind`): a new permalink, or one that moved. Run `ascribe permalinks sync`, or take the editor's quick fix, and commit the list with the change. Moving a permalink to another page changes one line of the list and removes nothing. Deleting one is a warning (`permalink-removed`), which `sync` doesn't clear: restore the name, or retire it ([Moving, aliasing, and retiring](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/astro/#moving-aliasing-and-retiring)). ### Moving, aliasing, and retiring A permalink is a promise to whatever links to it, so what to do when its section changes depends on what happened to the section: - **It moved,** to another page or under another heading: move the `@id` with it, and run `ascribe permalinks sync`. The address leads to the new place, and nothing else changes. - **It has a second name,** such as one an older release of the product prints: add an alias in [`[permalinks.aliases]`](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/content-model/#20-permalinks), `config = "weave-config"`. The alias's address leads where the permalink's does, and `verify` accepts both names. - **It's gone,** merged into another section or removed with the feature it described: retire it, with a reason a reader can understand. ```sh ascribe permalinks retire rotate-keys --reason "Merged into the security guide" --to guides/security.md ascribe permalinks retire legacy-sync --reason "The sync agent was removed in 4.0" ``` [`ascribe permalinks retire`](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/cli/#cli-permalinks-retire) writes each to `[permalinks.retired]` in `ascribe.toml`, keeping the file's comments, and records it in `ascribe.permalinks`, so `ascribe check` no longer warns. With `--to`, its address leads there; without it, the address is a page that says what was there was removed from the docs, gives the reason, and links to the docs' home page. A product's `verify` then fails on the name, with the reason, so the product changes its link. In the editor, the quick fix on `permalink-removed` writes the entry with a placeholder reason, which is an error until you replace it. To retire every permalink on a page you're about to delete, run it with `--page` before deleting the page. Retire rather than delete the line from the list: a deleted line makes the address a 404 with nothing to say why, and a product's `verify` says only that the name is missing. ### A permalink that isn't here A product released before a section was renamed, or after one was added, may link to a name these docs don't have. The host answers with the site's 404 page, as for any missing address, so put `MissingPermalink` on it: ```astro --- // src/pages/404.astro import MissingPermalink from "@ascribed/astro/MissingPermalink.astro"; --- <h1>Page not found</h1> <MissingPermalink /> ``` On an address under the permalinks' path, it says the link came from a product that expected a section of the docs there, names it, and offers the site's home page and search. Anywhere else, and without a script, it shows nothing. `home` sets where it sends the reader, the site's root by default; children replace its last paragraph, such as to point at your search: ```astro <MissingPermalink> <p>Search the docs for what you need, or go back to the <a href="/docs">home page</a>.</p> </MissingPermalink> ``` ## Review in the site preview Available: Ascribe (GA, 0.2.0+) In `astro dev`, Astro's dev toolbar has an **Ascribe review** app. It shows a pull request's changes and review comments on the real page, in your site's layout: the same marks and threads as the editor's [page preview](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/editor/#review-in-the-preview), from the same [`@ascribed/review`](https://github.com/ascribed-dev/ascribe/blob/main/packages/review/README.md) overlay. Nothing runs until you open the app: opening it starts review, and after **Stop Review**, the panel offers **Start Review**. [Review](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/review/) walks through reviewing a pull request with it; this section is the reference for the site's side. The app's panel sits above the toolbar, in one row: the pull request and the base (**#12 against main**), your place in the changes ("3 of 10 on this page", click it for the breakdown), **Changes / As it will be / As it was**, next and previous change, **Comments**, **Refresh**, and **More review actions** (**⋯**), whose **Prompt agent** items copy a prompt for your agent about the page's changes or a fragment's pages ([In review](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/agents/#in-review)). Each thread's **Prompt agent** copies one about its comment. Past the last change it offers the next changed page, by its title. When `ascribe check` finds errors in the working tree, the panel says how many, since a page with an error may not show as it will once it's fixed ([`ascribe diff`](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/cli/#cli-diff) explains why). Close it to get the page back; it stays closed or open as you move between pages, and review stays on until **Stop Review** or until `astro dev` stops. With the panel closed, a dot on the toolbar button says you have comments you haven't submitted. Starting review compares the checkout with the base of its branch's pull request, or, with no pull request, with the default branch (the first of `origin/HEAD`, `origin/main`, `origin/master`, `main`, and `master` that exists), from where the branch left it, as [`ascribe diff`](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/cli/#cli-diff) does. It compares again after each rebuild, so the marks follow your edits on save. Comments, replies, and resolving work as in the [page preview](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/editor/#preview), and [map to the pull request](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/review/#how-comments-map-to-the-pull-request) the same way: new comments are unsent until **Submit review…** in the panel sends them. Each mark's label and each thread's **Open source** opens the file at the line in your editor, through Vite's open-in-editor: set `LAUNCH_EDITOR` (for example, `LAUNCH_EDITOR=code`) to choose which. Comments need the [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com), signed in (`gh auth login`); the dev server runs it, and no token reaches the page. Without it, or without a pull request, the app shows the changes only and says why. The page and the dev server talk over Vite's own connection, which only pages from the dev server can open. If your Vite config loosens that (`server.cors: true`, `server.allowedHosts: true`, or `legacy.skipWebSocketTokenCheck`), any web page open in your browser could use it, so the app keeps comments off and says which setting to change. It keeps them off too when the dev server listens on the network (`astro dev --host`, or a `server.host` other than localhost), where anyone who can reach the site could comment as you; the changes still show. The marks, the threads, and the panel are light or dark as the page is, not as your system is, so a light-only site stays readable when your system is in dark mode. The app reads the page's background (or, with none, its `color-scheme`) and sets `data-ascribe-scheme` on the root element; a site that sets `data-ascribe-scheme="light"` or `"dark"` there itself keeps its own. Review is on for the whole dev server, not one tab: once you start it, every page of the site that loads, in any tab or browser, shows the marks and threads without a click, until **Stop Review**. Two pages have nothing to place: - **A route that isn't an Ascribe page** (a changelog page of your own, an index) says so, and lists the pages the change touches, each a link. - **A page whose layout drops the anchors**: the marks are placed by the `data-ascribe-source` attributes on each block, so a layout or component that rebuilds the content without them leaves nothing to mark. The panel says so, and lists the page's changes and threads instead, each with **Open source**. Comparing again after a save runs `ascribe diff` once, which takes about as long as an `ascribe build` of the project: under 50 ms on `examples/astro-site`. `astro dev` logs how long the first comparison took when review starts. ## Styling The elements render into the page (no shadow DOM), so your site's styles apply to them, and they're themed with CSS custom properties such as `--ascribe-tip-color` and `--ascribe-tab-active-color`. The [element library's README](https://github.com/ascribed-dev/ascribe/blob/main/packages/elements/README.md#theming) lists them, and shows how to style your own note types and lifecycle states. Their names don't change, but their default colors are Ascribe's and may change in a release, as the changelog notes, so set the ones your site needs fixed. ### Code block titles Available: Ascribe (GA, 0.2.0+) A code block's title, such as a [`@snippet`](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/directives/#snippet)'s `title`, is in its info string (` ```mjs title="astro.config.mjs" `). Astro's highlighting ignores it, so the integration adds a Shiki transformer that puts a titled block in a figure with the title as its caption: ```html <figure class="code-title"> <figcaption>astro.config.mjs</figcaption> <pre class="astro-code">…</pre> </figure> ``` The figure has your browser's default margins, and the caption no style of its own; style `figure.code-title` and its `figcaption` to suit your site. Titles need Astro's default highlight

Write `ascribe.toml` 30 31 Put `ascribe.toml` in the Astro project's root, beside `astro.config.mjs`. Its `[consumer]` settings must agree with Astro's `site`, `base`, and `trailingSlash`, because Ascribe writes every link: 32 33 ```toml 34 spec = "0.1" 35 36 [project] 37 content-root = "content" 38 output-dir = ".ascribe/build" 39 40 # Must agree with `astro.config.mjs`: `@ascribed/astro` checks that it does. 41 [consumer] 42 profile = "astro" 43 site = "https://docs.example.com" 44 base-path = "/docs/" 45 trailing-slash = "never" 46 ``` 47 48 The source pages go in `content/`. If your Ascribe project lives elsewhere, such as in a folder beside the site's, set the integration's `project` option to its directory (step 3). The [`ascribe.toml` reference](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/content-model/) has everything else it can declare. 49 50 ### 3\. Changes are batched, and builds run one at a time. 222 - After a successful rebuild, Astro reloads the collection and the page. 223 - After a failed one, the diagnostics are in Astro's terminal, and pages answer with HTTP 503 until a save builds cleanly again, so you never see a stale page. 224 - A change to `[project] output-dir` needs a restart of `astro dev`, and says so. 225 - Available: Ascribe (GA, 0.2.0+) 226 227 It writes where it's running (`url` and `build`) to `.ascribe/dev.json` in the project, for the editor's [Open Site Preview](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/editor/#site-preview), and removes the file when it stops. 228 229 ## Publish for AI agents 230 231 Available: Ascribe (in main, not yet released) 232 233 An AI agent reading your docs does better with Markdown than with HTML, and with an index to choose pages from. Turn on the outputs for agents in `ascribe.toml`'s `[consumer]`, beside `site`, and each build publishes them with the site, as the [Web Documentation Delivery Spec](https://agentdocsspec.com/spec/web/) lays them out: 234 235 ```toml 236 # llms.txt, a Markdown version of each page, and a pointer to the index on 237 # each: what agents read. `@ascribed/astro` publishes them with the site. 238 agents = true 239 ``` 240 241 - **`llms.txt`** at the base path: every page, by folder, as its title, a link to its Markdown, and its description (the field its type marks `role = "description"`). Past 50,000 characters it's split into one `llms.txt` per folder, which the root file links to. 242 - **Each page's Markdown** at its URL with `.md`: `/docs/guides/setup` is also `/docs/guides/setup.md`. 243 - **A pointer** at the top of each page to both, which the elements' stylesheet hides from sight but not from an agent reading the page. 244 245 `site` is required, because everything an agent reads links by absolute URL. The integration builds the plain output too, copies it into the built site, and serves it in `astro dev`. The [`ascribe.toml` reference](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/content-model/#15-consumer) says how `llms.txt` is put together. 246 247 `ascribe check` then adds two pieces of advice: a page whose description is too long for its line in `llms.txt`, and an `llms.txt` that's still too long when split. Write each page's `description` as one sentence saying what the page is for; it's what an agent picks a page by. 248 249 ### What your host does 250 251 The files are static, so any host serves them. A few things the spec asks are the server's, not the build's: 252 253 - **The `.md` files' type.** Serve them as `text/markdown; charset=utf-8`, and `llms.txt` as `text/plain; charset=utf-8`, as `astro dev` does. Check what your host sends (`curl -I` a page's `.md`), and set the header in its configuration if it's something else. 254 - **Content negotiation.** An agent may ask for a page with `Accept: text/markdown`; answering it with the page's `.md` needs a rule on the server, such as an edge function or middleware that rewrites to `<path>.md` when that header asks for Markdown. Without it, agents still find the `.md` URLs through `llms.txt` and the pointer. On Netlify, an edge function does it: this site's is [`markdown.ts`](https://github.com/ascribed-dev/ascribe/blob/main/site/netlify/edge-functions/markdown.ts). 255 - **Status codes and caching.** A missing page should answer 404, not 200 with a page saying so, and the `.md` files and `llms.txt` should be cached no longer than the pages. 256 - **Bot protection.** A rule that challenges unfamiliar clients blocks agents too; let them read `llms.txt` and the `.md` files. 257 258 ## Permalinks 259 260 Available: Ascribe (in main, not yet released) 261 262 A heading marked as a [permalink](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/directives/#permalinks), `@id {permalink=true}: weave-config`, gets an address of its own, `go/weave-config` under the base path, which sends the reader to the heading wherever it is now. A page with `permalink: options` in its frontmatter gets `go/options`, which leads to the top of the page. Link to that address from outside the docs, such as from your product's interface or its error messages, and the link keeps working when the page moves. 263 264 The integration adds the route itself, from the list each build writes (`_ascribe/permalinks.json` in the site output, [output-layout contract §1.2](https://ascribed-dev.com/contracts/output-layout/#12-the-permalinks-list)). Each address is a small page that: 265 266 - forwards at once with a `<meta http-equiv="refresh">`, without a script, keeping a heading's anchor; 267 - with a script, first takes the reader's choices from the address's parameters ([Linking from a product](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/astro/#linking-from-a-product)); 268 - links to the same place, for a browser that doesn't follow; 269 - is marked `noindex`, with a canonical link to where it leads, so search engines list the page and not the address. 270 271 So it works on any static host, in `astro build` and in `astro dev`, where a permalink you add or remove is served on the next rebuild, with no restart. The addresses end the way the site's routes do (`trailing-slash`), and aren't pages of the collection, `llms.txt`, or the Markdown for agents. 272 273 [`permalink-path`](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/content-model/#15-consumer) moves them, as a path from the site's root, such as `"/go/"` when the docs move under `/docs/` but the addresses your product prints shouldn't. It must be under Astro's `base`, since that's all an Astro site serves; the integration fails the build when it isn't. 274 275 **With another generator,** read `_ascribe/permalinks.json` from the build's site output and publish a page like these at `path` and each name, forwarding to `route`, and `#` and `fragment` for a heading. For the parameters, its script calls `@ascribed/elements`' `choose` for each one that names a [dimension](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/content-model/#6-dimensionsname) in the list's `dimensions` with one of its values, then forwards. A host's redirect rules can do the same as the page without its script, but a redirect drops nothing only if the host keeps the anchor. 276 277 ### Linking from a product 278 279 A product links to a permalink's address: the site, the permalinks' path, and the name, ending the way the site's routes do. It can add what it knows about its reader, as parameters named for the content model's [dimensions](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/content-model/#6-dimensionsname): 280 281 ```ts 282 // The docs' permalinks, as `[consumer]` publishes them. 283 const permalinks = "https://docs.example.com/docs/go/"; 284 285 function docsLink(name: string, reader: Record<string, string> = {}): string { 286 const url = new URL(name, permalinks); 287 for (const [dimension, value] of Object.entries(reader)) url.searchParams.set(dimension, value); 288 return url.href; 289 } 290 291 // https://docs.example.com/docs/go/weave-config?pm=pnpm 292 docsLink("weave-config", { pm: "pnpm" }); 293 ``` 294 295 - **A parameter that names a dimension, with one of its values,** sets the reader's choice for that dimension, as if they'd picked the tab: the section opens with the `pnpm` tab showing, and the choice holds on the pages they read next. 296 - **Anything else is ignored:** a name that isn't a dimension, or a value the dimension doesn't have. Send what the product knows, without checking what the docs accept; a link with only unknown parameters works as one with none. 297 - **The choice needs a script and the browser's storage.** With scripts off, the address forwards to the section with the tabs as they were; with storage blocked, the choice doesn't reach the next page. 298 - **A version isn't a parameter yet.** `self-managed=3.4` is ignored like any unknown one. 299 300 ### Checking a product's links 301 302 A product that links to the docs can check, in its own CI, that every name it links to is still a permalink there, without building or even having the docs. The docs commit their list of permalinks, `ascribe.permalinks`, which `ascribe permalinks sync` writes beside `ascribe.toml` ([The permalinks list](https://ascribed-dev.com/contracts/permalinks-list/)). Then `ascribe check` in the docs warns when a permalink is removed, and the product checks its names against a copy of the list: 303 304 ```yaml 305 # .github/workflows/docs-links.yml, in the product's repository 306 name: Docs links 307 on: [pull_request] 308 jobs: 309 docs-links: 310 runs-on: ubuntu-latest 311 steps: 312 - uses: actions/checkout@v4 313 # The docs' list, from their repository; or keep a copy in this one. 314 - run: curl -fsSL -o docs.permalinks https://raw.githubusercontent.com/example/docs/main/ascribe.permalinks 315 - run: npx @ascribed/cli permalinks verify --list docs.permalinks --from docs-links.txt 316 ``` 317 318 `docs-links.txt` lists the names the product links to, one on each line. [`ascribe permalinks verify`](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/cli/#cli-permalinks-verify) exits with 1, naming each name the list doesn't have, and each the docs retired, with the reason they gave, so a link to a section the docs removed, or never had, fails the product's pull request rather than reaching its users. An alias passes, as the permalink it leads to does. 319 320 In the docs, `ascribe check` reports a list that's behind the content (`permalinks-list-behind`): a new permalink, or one that moved. Run `ascribe permalinks sync`, or take the editor's quick fix, and commit the list with the change. Moving a permalink to another page changes one line of the list and removes nothing. Deleting one is a warning (`permalink-removed`), which `sync` doesn't clear: restore the name, or retire it ([Moving, aliasing, and retiring](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/astro/#moving-aliasing-and-retiring)). 321 322 ### Moving, aliasing, and retiring 323 324 A permalink is a promise to whatever links to it, so what to do when its section changes depends on what happened to the section: 325 326 - **It moved,** to another page or under another heading: move the `@id` with it, and run `ascribe permalinks sync`. The address leads to the new place, and nothing else changes. 327 - **It has a second name,** such as one an older release of the product prints: add an alias in [`[permalinks.aliases]`](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/content-model/#20-permalinks), `config = "weave-config"`. The alias's address leads where the permalink's does, and `verify` accepts both names. 328 - **It's gone,** merged into another section or removed with the feature it described: retire it, with a reason a reader can understand. 329 330 ```sh 331 ascribe permalinks retire rotate-keys --reason "Merged into the security guide" --to guides/security.md 332 ascribe permalinks retire legacy-sync --reason "The sync agent was removed in 4.0" 333 ``` 334 335 [`ascribe permalinks retire`](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/cli/#cli-permalinks-retire) writes each to `[permalinks.retired]` in `ascribe.toml`, keeping the file's comments, and records it in `ascribe.permalinks`, so `ascribe check` no longer warns. With `--to`, its address leads there; without it, the address is a page that says what was there was removed from the docs, gives the reason, and links to the docs' home page. A product's `verify` then fails on the name, with the reason, so the product changes its link. In the editor, the quick fix on `permalink-removed` writes the entry with a placeholder reason, which is an error until you replace it. To retire every permalink on a page you're about to delete, run it with `--page` before deleting the page. 336 337 Retire rather than delete the line from the list: a deleted line makes the address a 404 with nothing to say why, and a product's `verify` says only that the name is missing. 338 339 ### A permalink that isn't here 340 341 A product released before a section was renamed, or after one was added, may link to a name these docs don't have. The host answers with the site's 404 page, as for any missing address, so put `MissingPermalink` on it: 342 343 ```astro 344 --- 345 // src/pages/404.astro 346 import MissingPermalink from "@ascribed/astro/MissingPermalink.astro"; 347 --- 348 349 <h1>Page not found</h1> 350 <MissingPermalink /> 351 ``` 352 353 On an address under the permalinks' path, it says the link came from a product that expected a section of the docs there, names it, and offers the site's home page and search. Anywhere else, and without a script, it shows nothing. `home` sets where it sends the reader, the site's root by default; children replace its last paragraph, such as to point at your search: 354 355 ```astro 356 <MissingPermalink> 357 <p>Search the docs for what you need, or go back to the <a href="/docs">home page</a>.</p> 358 </MissingPermalink> 359 ``` 360 361 ## Review in the site preview 362 363 Available: Ascribe (GA, 0.2.0+) 364 365 In `astro dev`, Astro's dev toolbar has an **Ascribe review** app. It shows a pull request's changes and review comments on the real page, in your site's layout: the same marks and threads as the editor's [page preview](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/editor/#review-in-the-preview), from the same [`@ascribed/review`](https://github.com/ascribed-dev/ascribe/blob/main/packages/review/README.md) overlay. Nothing runs until you open the app: opening it starts review, and after **Stop Review**, the panel offers **Start Review**. [Review](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/review/) walks through reviewing a pull request with it; this section is the reference for the site's side. 366 367 The app's panel sits above the toolbar, in one row: the pull request and the base (**#12 against main**), your place in the changes ("3 of 10 on this page", click it for the breakdown), **Changes / As it will be / As it was**, next and previous change, **Comments**, **Refresh**, and **More review actions** (**⋯**), whose **Prompt agent** items copy a prompt for your agent about the page's changes or a fragment's pages ([In review](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/agents/#in-review)). When `ascribe check` finds errors in the working tree, the panel says how many, since a page with an error may not show as it will once it's fixed ([`ascribe diff`](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/cli/#cli-diff) explains why). Close it to get the page back; it stays closed or open as you move between pages, and review stays on until **Stop Review** or until `astro dev` stops. With the panel closed, a dot on the toolbar button says you have comments you haven't submitted. 368 369 Starting review compares the checkout with the base of its branch's pull request, or, with no pull request, with the default branch (the first of `origin/HEAD`, `origin/main`, `origin/master`, `main`, and `master` that exists), from where the branch left it, as [`ascribe diff`](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/cli/#cli-diff) does. It compares again after each rebuild, so the marks follow your edits on save. Comments, replies, and resolving work as in the [page preview](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/editor/#preview), and [map to the pull request](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/review/#how-comments-map-to-the-pull-request) the same way: new comments are unsent until **Submit review…** in the panel sends them. Each mark's label and each thread's **Open source** opens the file at the line in your editor, through Vite's open-in-editor: set `LAUNCH_EDITOR` (for example, `LAUNCH_EDITOR=code`) to choose which. 370 371 Comments need the [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com), signed in (`gh auth login`); the dev server runs it, and no token reaches the page. Without it, or without a pull request, the app shows the changes only and says why. The page and the dev server talk over Vite's own connection, which only pages from the dev server can open. If your Vite config loosens that (`server.cors: true`, `server.allowedHosts: true`, or `legacy.skipWebSocketTokenCheck`), any web page open in your browser could use it, so the app keeps comments off and says which setting to change. It keeps them off too when the dev server listens on the network (`astro dev --host`, or a `server.host` other than localhost), where anyone who can reach the site could comment as you; the changes still show. 372 373 The marks, the threads, and the panel are light or dark as the page is, not as your system is, so a light-only site stays readable when your system is in dark mode. The app reads the page's background (or, with none, its `color-scheme`) and sets `data-ascribe-scheme` on the root element; a site that sets `data-ascribe-scheme="light"` or `"dark"` there itself keeps its own. 374 375 Review is on for the whole dev server, not one tab: once you start it, every page of the site that loads, in any tab or browser, shows the marks and threads without a click, until **Stop Review**. 376 377 Two pages have nothing to place: 378 379 - **A route that isn't an Ascribe page** (a changelog page of your own, an index) says so, and lists the pages the change touches, each a link. 380 - **A page whose layout drops the anchors**: the marks are placed by the `data-ascribe-source` attributes on each block, so a layout or component that rebuilds the content without them leaves nothing to mark. The panel says so, and lists the page's changes and threads instead, each with **Open source**. 381 382 Comparing again after a save runs `ascribe diff` once, which takes about as long as an `ascribe build` of the project: under 50 ms on `examples/astro-site`. `astro dev` logs how long the first comparison took when review starts. 383 384 ## Styling 385 386 The elements render into the page (no shadow DOM), so your site's styles apply to them, and they're themed with CSS custom properties such as `--ascribe-tip-color` and `--ascribe-tab-active-color`. The [element library's README](https://github.com/ascribed-dev/ascribe/blob/main/packages/elements/README.md#theming) lists them, and shows how to style your own note types and lifecycle states. Their names don't change, but their default colors are Ascribe's and may change in a release, as the changelog notes, so set the ones your site needs fixed. 387 388 ### Code block titles 389 390 Available: Ascribe (GA, 0.2.0+) 391 392 A code block's title, such as a [`@snippet`](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/directives/#snippet)'s `title`, is in its info string (` ```mjs title="astro.config.mjs" `). Astro's highlighting ignores it, so the integration adds a Shiki transformer that puts a titled block in a figure with the title as its caption: 393 394 ```html 395 <figure class="code-title"> 396 <figcaption>astro.config.mjs</figcaption> 397 <pre class="astro-code">…</pre> 398 </figure> 399 ``` 400 401 The figure has your browser's default margins, and the caption no style of its own; style `figure.code-title` and its `figcaption` to suit your site. Titles need Astro's default highlighting, Shiki; with `syntaxHighlight: "prism"` or `false`, they aren't shown. 402 403 ## Other Markdown processors 404 405 The integration supports Astro's default processor (Sätteri) and `unified()`. Any other processor is an error at startup, since heading ids and image attributes would be lost. 406

> For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ascribed-dev.com/llms.txt). # Astro `@ascribed/astro` publishes an Ascribe project as an [Astro](https://astro.build) site. It runs `ascribe build --emit site` before Astro loads content, gives you a content collection of the built pages with a schema generated from `ascribe.toml`, applies heading ids and image attributes in Astro's own Markdown pipeline (so Astro's table of contents and image processing still work), loads the element library, and serves the files pages link to. In `astro dev`, it rebuilds as you edit. It supports Astro 7.3.5 and later 7.x releases. ## Set up a site These steps add Ascribe to an Astro project. [`examples/astro-site`](https://github.com/ascribed-dev/ascribe/tree/main/examples/astro-site) is a complete site built this way. ### 1\. Install **npm** ```sh npm install @ascribed/astro ``` **pnpm** ```sh pnpm add @ascribed/astro ``` It brings `@ascribed/cli`, the `ascribe` command for your platform, and `@ascribed/elements`. Astro's image processing also needs `sharp` (`npm install sharp`) if your project doesn't have it. ### 2\. Write `ascribe.toml` Put `ascribe.toml` in the Astro project's root, beside `astro.config.mjs`. Its `[consumer]` settings must agree with Astro's `site`, `base`, and `trailingSlash`, because Ascribe writes every link: ```toml spec = "0.1" [project] content-root = "content" output-dir = ".ascribe/build" # Must agree with `astro.config.mjs`: `@ascribed/astro` checks that it does. [consumer] profile = "astro" site = "https://docs.example.com" base-path = "/docs/" trailing-slash = "never" ``` The source pages go in `content/`. If your Ascribe project lives elsewhere, such as in a folder beside the site's, set the integration's `project` option to its directory (step 3). The [`ascribe.toml` reference](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/content-model/) has everything else it can declare. ### 3\. Add the integration ```mjs title="astro.config.mjs" import { defineConfig } from "astro/config"; import ascribe from "@ascribed/astro"; // `site`, `base`, and `trailingSlash` repeat ascribe.toml's [consumer]; the // integration fails the build if they disagree. export default defineConfig({ site: "https://docs.example.com", base: "/docs", trailingSlash: "never", integrations: [ascribe({ build: "site" })], }); ``` `build` names the [build](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/content-model/#16-buildsname) in `ascribe.toml` whose output the site shows. A project without `[builds]` has one, `site`. ### 4\. Define the collection ```ts title="src/content.config.ts" import { defineCollection } from "astro:content"; import { ascribeCollection } from "@ascribed/astro/content"; // Generated by `ascribe build --emit site`; the integration runs it first. import { schema } from "../.ascribe/build/site/site/_ascribe/schema.ts"; export const collections = { docs: defineCollection(ascribeCollection({ schema })), }; ``` The schema's path is `//site/_ascribe/schema.ts`, in the directory holding `ascribe.toml`. Importing it by path keeps its exact types, so `entry.data` is typed from your content types. If you change `[project] output-dir`, the build, or the integration's `project`, change this line too. Available: Ascribe (GA, 0.2.0+) If the Ascribe project is outside the Astro root (`project: "../docs"`), import the copy of the schema the integration writes inside it instead, `.astro/integrations/_ascribed_astro/schema.ts`, which is `../.astro/integrations/_ascribed_astro/schema.ts` from `src/content.config.ts`. The schema imports `astro/zod`, which TypeScript can only find from inside the Astro project, so type-checking (`astro check`, `tsc`) fails on the original there; Astro's own build works with either. The integration updates the copy after each build. ### 5\. Add a route A page's URL is the base path plus its entry id, and the root page, `content/index.md` (entry id `index`), is at the base path itself. That's what Ascribe's links point to: ```astro title="src/pages/[...slug].astro" --- import { getCollection, render } from "astro:content"; import Docs from "../layouts/Docs.astro"; // A page's route is the base path plus its entry id, and the root page (id // `index`) is at the base path itself: what Ascribe's router computes for // every link it writes. export async function getStaticPaths() { const entries = await getCollection("docs"); return entries.map((entry) => ({ params: { slug: entry.id === "index" ? undefined : entry.id }, props: { entry }, })); } const { entry } = Astro.props; const { Content, headings } = await render(entry); --- ``` Entry ids are Astro's own: `Guides/My Setup.md` is `guides/my-setup`. ### 6\. Load the elements in your layout A layout loads the element library and shows the page's availability: Available: Ascribe (GA, 0.2.0+) ```astro title="src/layouts/Docs.astro" --- import type { CollectionEntry } from "astro:content"; import Availability from "@ascribed/astro/Availability.astro"; import Elements from "@ascribed/astro/Elements.astro"; interface Props { entry: CollectionEntry<"docs">; headings: { depth: number; slug: string; text: string }[]; } const { entry, headings } = Astro.props; // `title` is plain text; `formatted.title` is the title as HTML, with its // code spans as , because the content model sets `inline = "code"`. const { title, formatted, description, available } = entry.data; --- {title} {description && }

    { headings.map((heading) => (
  • {heading.text}
    • )) }

``` `` loads the element library's stylesheet and the small script `` needs. The layout is yours: the page title, navigation, and table of contents (`headings` from `render`) come from your own components. Available: Ascribe (GA, 0.2.0+) The example's [content model](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/content-model/) sets `inline = "code"` on `title`, so a title can show code, as "`` `loom.yaml` options ``". `entry.data.title` is then plain text, for `` and search, and `entry.data.formatted.title` is the title as HTML, with each code span a `<code>`, for the heading and navigation (`set:html`). Without the setting, there's no `formatted`: use `title` everywhere. See [code in a field](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/content-model/#53-code-in-a-field). A page's `available` frontmatter reaches the layout as `entry.data.available`: a list of targets, each with the text to show. Available: Ascribe (GA, 0.2.0+) `<Availability available={entry.data.available} />`, from `@ascribed/astro/Availability.astro`, renders it as a badge, as the layout above does: the same markup the site output gives a section's `@available`, which the element library styles. It renders nothing for a page with no availability. In a release without `Availability.astro`, copy [its markup](https://github.com/ascribed-dev/ascribe/blob/main/packages/astro/src/Availability.astro) into your layout in place of the component. ### 7\. Build ```sh npx astro dev # rebuilds as you edit npx astro build ``` ## Options | Option | Meaning | | --- | --- | | `build` | The build whose site output is the collection: a build name in `ascribe.toml`. Required. | | `project` | The directory holding `ascribe.toml`, relative to the Astro root. By default, the root. | | `binary` | The `ascribe` binary to run, relative to the Astro root. By default, the `ASCRIBE_BIN` environment variable, then the binary `@ascribed/cli` installed. | | `anchors` (Available: Ascribe (GA, 0.2.0+)) | Mark each block of the page with the source file and lines it came from (`data-ascribe-source`; see the [site-render contract](https://ascribed-dev.com/contracts/site-render/#7-source-anchors)), for review: `"dev"` in `astro dev` only, `true` in `astro build` too. Use `"dev"` unless the build is for reviewers: `true` puts source file paths, [fragments](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/directives/#files)' included, in the published pages. By default, `false`, though `review` turns them on in `astro dev`. | | `review` (Available: Ascribe (GA, 0.2.0+)) | [Review in the site preview](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/astro/#review-in-the-site-preview): the **Ascribe review** app in `astro dev`'s toolbar. `false` leaves it out. By default, `true`. `astro build` never has it. | | `codeTitles` (Available: Ascribe (GA, 0.2.0+)) | Show a code block's title above it ([code block titles](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/astro/#code-block-titles)). `false` leaves titles out, for a site that shows them itself. By default, `true`. | ## What the integration does - **Fails the Astro build** when `ascribe build` reports an error (the compiler's report is the error), and when `ascribe.toml`'s `[consumer]` `site`, `base-path`, or `trailing-slash` disagrees with Astro's `site`, `base`, or `trailingSlash`. Astro's `trailingSlash: "ignore"` agrees with either value. - **Adds its Markdown plugin** to Astro's Markdown processor, to apply heading ids, image attributes, glossary terms' `data-ascribe-term`, and source anchors: to the default Sätteri processor's `hastPlugins`, or to a `unified()` processor's `rehypePlugins`. Both plugins are exported, as `@ascribed/astro/satteri` and `@ascribed/astro/rehype`, for a processor you configure yourself. Their types come from `satteri` and `@types/hast`, optional peer dependencies: a Sätteri processor already has the first, and a `unified()` one the second. - **Serves the files pages link to** (other than pages and images) at `<base>_ascribe/files/`, in `astro dev` and in the built site. - Available: Ascribe (in main, not yet released) **Publishes the outputs for agents** with `[consumer] agents = true`: `llms.txt` and each page's Markdown, in `astro dev` and in the built site ([Publish for AI agents](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/astro/#publish-for-ai-agents)). - Available: Ascribe (in main, not yet released) **Gives each permalink an address** that forwards to its page or heading, in `astro dev` and in the built site ([Permalinks](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/astro/#permalinks)). - Available: Ascribe (GA, 0.2.0+) **Shows code block titles**, with a Shiki transformer it adds to Astro's code highlighting ([code block titles](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/astro/#code-block-titles)). - Available: Ascribe (GA, 0.2.0+) **Copies the generated schema** into `.astro/integrations/_ascribed_astro/schema.ts` after each build, for a project outside the Astro root ([step 4](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/astro/#4-define-the-collection)). ### In `astro dev` - Saving a page, a fragment, an image or other file under the content root, an asset elsewhere in the project that a page uses, or `ascribe.toml` rebuilds. Changes are batched, and builds run one at a time. - After a successful rebuild, Astro reloads the collection and the page. - After a failed one, the diagnostics are in Astro's terminal, and pages answer with HTTP 503 until a save builds cleanly again, so you never see a stale page. - A change to `[project] output-dir` needs a restart of `astro dev`, and says so. - Available: Ascribe (GA, 0.2.0+) It writes where it's running (`url` and `build`) to `.ascribe/dev.json` in the project, for the editor's [Open Site Preview](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/editor/#site-preview), and removes the file when it stops. ## Publish for AI agents Available: Ascribe (in main, not yet released) An AI agent reading your docs does better with Markdown than with HTML, and with an index to choose pages from. Turn on the outputs for agents in `ascribe.toml`'s `[consumer]`, beside `site`, and each build publishes them with the site, as the [Web Documentation Delivery Spec](https://agentdocsspec.com/spec/web/) lays them out: ```toml # llms.txt, a Markdown version of each page, and a pointer to the index on # each: what agents read. `@ascribed/astro` publishes them with the site. agents = true ``` - **`llms.txt`** at the base path: every page, by folder, as its title, a link to its Markdown, and its description (the field its type marks `role = "description"`). Past 50,000 characters it's split into one `llms.txt` per folder, which the root file links to. - **Each page's Markdown** at its URL with `.md`: `/docs/guides/setup` is also `/docs/guides/setup.md`. - **A pointer** at the top of each page to both, which the elements' stylesheet hides from sight but not from an agent reading the page. `site` is required, because everything an agent reads links by absolute URL. The integration builds the plain output too, copies it into the built site, and serves it in `astro dev`. The [`ascribe.toml` reference](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/content-model/#15-consumer) says how `llms.txt` is put together. `ascribe check` then adds two pieces of advice: a page whose description is too long for its line in `llms.txt`, and an `llms.txt` that's still too long when split. Write each page's `description` as one sentence saying what the page is for; it's what an agent picks a page by. ### What your host does The files are static, so any host serves them. A few things the spec asks are the server's, not the build's: - **The `.md` files' type.** Serve them as `text/markdown; charset=utf-8`, and `llms.txt` as `text/plain; charset=utf-8`, as `astro dev` does. Check what your host sends (`curl -I` a page's `.md`), and set the header in its configuration if it's something else. - **Content negotiation.** An agent may ask for a page with `Accept: text/markdown`; answering it with the page's `.md` needs a rule on the server, such as an edge function or middleware that rewrites to `<path>.md` when that header asks for Markdown. Without it, agents still find the `.md` URLs through `llms.txt` and the pointer. On Netlify, an edge function does it: this site's is [`markdown.ts`](https://github.com/ascribed-dev/ascribe/blob/main/site/netlify/edge-functions/markdown.ts). - **Status codes and caching.** A missing page should answer 404, not 200 with a page saying so, and the `.md` files and `llms.txt` should be cached no longer than the pages. - **Bot protection.** A rule that challenges unfamiliar clients blocks agents too; let them read `llms.txt` and the `.md` files. ## Permalinks Available: Ascribe (in main, not yet released) A heading marked as a [permalink](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/directives/#permalinks), `@id {permalink=true}: weave-config`, gets an address of its own, `go/weave-config` under the base path, which sends the reader to the heading wherever it is now. A page with `permalink: options` in its frontmatter gets `go/options`, which leads to the top of the page. Link to that address from outside the docs, such as from your product's interface or its error messages, and the link keeps working when the page moves. The integration adds the route itself, from the list each build writes (`_ascribe/permalinks.json` in the site output, [output-layout contract §1.2](https://ascribed-dev.com/contracts/output-layout/#12-the-permalinks-list)). Each address is a small page that: - forwards at once with a `<meta http-equiv="refresh">`, without a script, keeping a heading's anchor; - with a script, first takes the reader's choices from the address's parameters ([Linking from a product](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/astro/#linking-from-a-product)); - links to the same place, for a browser that doesn't follow; - is marked `noindex`, with a canonical link to where it leads, so search engines list the page and not the address. So it works on any static host, in `astro build` and in `astro dev`, where a permalink you add or remove is served on the next rebuild, with no restart. The addresses end the way the site's routes do (`trailing-slash`), and aren't pages of the collection, `llms.txt`, or the Markdown for agents. [`permalink-path`](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/content-model/#15-consumer) moves them, as a path from the site's root, such as `"/go/"` when the docs move under `/docs/` but the addresses your product prints shouldn't. It must be under Astro's `base`, since that's all an Astro site serves; the integration fails the build when it isn't. **With another generator,** read `_ascribe/permalinks.json` from the build's site output and publish a page like these at `path` and each name, forwarding to `route`, and `#` and `fragment` for a heading. For the parameters, its script calls `@ascribed/elements`' `choose` for each one that names a [dimension](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/content-model/#6-dimensionsname) in the list's `dimensions` with one of its values, then forwards. A host's redirect rules can do the same as the page without its script, but a redirect drops nothing only if the host keeps the anchor. ### Linking from a product A product links to a permalink's address: the site, the permalinks' path, and the name, ending the way the site's routes do. It can add what it knows about its reader, as parameters named for the content model's [dimensions](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/content-model/#6-dimensionsname): ```ts // The docs' permalinks, as `[consumer]` publishes them. const permalinks = "https://docs.example.com/docs/go/"; function docsLink(name: string, reader: Record<string, string> = {}): string { const url = new URL(name, permalinks); for (const [dimension, value] of Object.entries(reader)) url.searchParams.set(dimension, value); return url.href; } // https://docs.example.com/docs/go/weave-config?pm=pnpm docsLink("weave-config", { pm: "pnpm" }); ``` - **A parameter that names a dimension, with one of its values,** sets the reader's choice for that dimension, as if they'd picked the tab: the section opens with the `pnpm` tab showing, and the choice holds on the pages they read next. - **Anything else is ignored:** a name that isn't a dimension, or a value the dimension doesn't have. Send what the product knows, without checking what the docs accept; a link with only unknown parameters works as one with none. - **The choice needs a script and the browser's storage.** With scripts off, the address forwards to the section with the tabs as they were; with storage blocked, the choice doesn't reach the next page. - **A version isn't a parameter yet.** `self-managed=3.4` is ignored like any unknown one. ### Checking a product's links A product that links to the docs can check, in its own CI, that every name it links to is still a permalink there, without building or even having the docs. The docs commit their list of permalinks, `ascribe.permalinks`, which `ascribe permalinks sync` writes beside `ascribe.toml` ([The permalinks list](https://ascribed-dev.com/contracts/permalinks-list/)). Then `ascribe check` in the docs warns when a permalink is removed, and the product checks its names against a copy of the list: ```yaml # .github/workflows/docs-links.yml, in the product's repository name: Docs links on: [pull_request] jobs: docs-links: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 # The docs' list, from their repository; or keep a copy in this one. - run: curl -fsSL -o docs.permalinks https://raw.githubusercontent.com/example/docs/main/ascribe.permalinks - run: npx @ascribed/cli permalinks verify --list docs.permalinks --from docs-links.txt ``` `docs-links.txt` lists the names the product links to, one on each line. [`ascribe permalinks verify`](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/cli/#cli-permalinks-verify) exits with 1, naming each name the list doesn't have, and each the docs retired, with the reason they gave, so a link to a section the docs removed, or never had, fails the product's pull request rather than reaching its users. An alias passes, as the permalink it leads to does. In the docs, `ascribe check` reports a list that's behind the content (`permalinks-list-behind`): a new permalink, or one that moved. Run `ascribe permalinks sync`, or take the editor's quick fix, and commit the list with the change. Moving a permalink to another page changes one line of the list and removes nothing. Deleting one is a warning (`permalink-removed`), which `sync` doesn't clear: restore the name, or retire it ([Moving, aliasing, and retiring](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/astro/#moving-aliasing-and-retiring)). ### Moving, aliasing, and retiring A permalink is a promise to whatever links to it, so what to do when its section changes depends on what happened to the section: - **It moved,** to another page or under another heading: move the `@id` with it, and run `ascribe permalinks sync`. The address leads to the new place, and nothing else changes. - **It has a second name,** such as one an older release of the product prints: add an alias in [`[permalinks.aliases]`](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/content-model/#20-permalinks), `config = "weave-config"`. The alias's address leads where the permalink's does, and `verify` accepts both names. - **It's gone,** merged into another section or removed with the feature it described: retire it, with a reason a reader can understand. ```sh ascribe permalinks retire rotate-keys --reason "Merged into the security guide" --to guides/security.md ascribe permalinks retire legacy-sync --reason "The sync agent was removed in 4.0" ``` [`ascribe permalinks retire`](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/cli/#cli-permalinks-retire) writes each to `[permalinks.retired]` in `ascribe.toml`, keeping the file's comments, and records it in `ascribe.permalinks`, so `ascribe check` no longer warns. With `--to`, its address leads there; without it, the address is a page that says what was there was removed from the docs, gives the reason, and links to the docs' home page. A product's `verify` then fails on the name, with the reason, so the product changes its link. In the editor, the quick fix on `permalink-removed` writes the entry with a placeholder reason, which is an error until you replace it. To retire every permalink on a page you're about to delete, run it with `--page` before deleting the page. Retire rather than delete the line from the list: a deleted line makes the address a 404 with nothing to say why, and a product's `verify` says only that the name is missing. ### A permalink that isn't here A product released before a section was renamed, or after one was added, may link to a name these docs don't have. The host answers with the site's 404 page, as for any missing address, so put `MissingPermalink` on it: ```astro --- // src/pages/404.astro import MissingPermalink from "@ascribed/astro/MissingPermalink.astro"; --- <h1>Page not found</h1> <MissingPermalink /> ``` On an address under the permalinks' path, it says the link came from a product that expected a section of the docs there, names it, and offers the site's home page and search. Anywhere else, and without a script, it shows nothing. `home` sets where it sends the reader, the site's root by default; children replace its last paragraph, such as to point at your search: ```astro <MissingPermalink> <p>Search the docs for what you need, or go back to the <a href="/docs">home page</a>.</p> </MissingPermalink> ``` ## Review in the site preview Available: Ascribe (GA, 0.2.0+) In `astro dev`, Astro's dev toolbar has an **Ascribe review** app. It shows a pull request's changes and review comments on the real page, in your site's layout: the same marks and threads as the editor's [page preview](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/editor/#review-in-the-preview), from the same [`@ascribed/review`](https://github.com/ascribed-dev/ascribe/blob/main/packages/review/README.md) overlay. Nothing runs until you open the app: opening it starts review, and after **Stop Review**, the panel offers **Start Review**. [Review](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/review/) walks through reviewing a pull request with it; this section is the reference for the site's side. The app's panel sits above the toolbar, in one row: the pull request and the base (**#12 against main**), your place in the changes ("3 of 10 on this page", click it for the breakdown), **Changes / As it will be / As it was**, next and previous change, **Comments**, **Refresh**, and **More review actions** (**⋯**), whose **Prompt agent** items copy a prompt for your agent about the page's changes or a fragment's pages ([In review](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/agents/#in-review)). Each thread's **Prompt agent** copies one about its comment. Past the last change it offers the next changed page, by its title. When `ascribe check` finds errors in the working tree, the panel says how many, since a page with an error may not show as it will once it's fixed ([`ascribe diff`](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/cli/#cli-diff) explains why). Close it to get the page back; it stays closed or open as you move between pages, and review stays on until **Stop Review** or until `astro dev` stops. With the panel closed, a dot on the toolbar button says you have comments you haven't submitted. Starting review compares the checkout with the base of its branch's pull request, or, with no pull request, with the default branch (the first of `origin/HEAD`, `origin/main`, `origin/master`, `main`, and `master` that exists), from where the branch left it, as [`ascribe diff`](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/cli/#cli-diff) does. It compares again after each rebuild, so the marks follow your edits on save. Comments, replies, and resolving work as in the [page preview](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/editor/#preview), and [map to the pull request](https://ascribed-dev.com/guides/review/#how-comments-map-to-the-pull-request) the same way: new comments are unsent until **Submit review…** in the panel sends them. Each mark's label and each thread's **Open source** opens the file at the line in your editor, through Vite's open-in-editor: set `LAUNCH_EDITOR` (for example, `LAUNCH_EDITOR=code`) to choose which. Comments need the [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com), signed in (`gh auth login`); the dev server runs it, and no token reaches the page. Without it, or without a pull request, the app shows the changes only and says why. The page and the dev server talk over Vite's own connection, which only pages from the dev server can open. If your Vite config loosens that (`server.cors: true`, `server.allowedHosts: true`, or `legacy.skipWebSocketTokenCheck`), any web page open in your browser could use it, so the app keeps comments off and says which setting to change. It keeps them off too when the dev server listens on the network (`astro dev --host`, or a `server.host` other than localhost), where anyone who can reach the site could comment as you; the changes still show. The marks, the threads, and the panel are light or dark as the page is, not as your system is, so a light-only site stays readable when your system is in dark mode. The app reads the page's background (or, with none, its `color-scheme`) and sets `data-ascribe-scheme` on the root element; a site that sets `data-ascribe-scheme="light"` or `"dark"` there itself keeps its own. Review is on for the whole dev server, not one tab: once you start it, every page of the site that loads, in any tab or browser, shows the marks and threads without a click, until **Stop Review**. Two pages have nothing to place: - **A route that isn't an Ascribe page** (a changelog page of your own, an index) says so, and lists the pages the change touches, each a link. - **A page whose layout drops the anchors**: the marks are placed by the `data-ascribe-source` attributes on each block, so a layout or component that rebuilds the content without them leaves nothing to mark. The panel says so, and lists the page's changes and threads instead, each with **Open source**. Comparing again after a save runs `ascribe diff` once, which takes about as long as an `ascribe build` of the project: under 50 ms on `examples/astro-site`. `astro dev` logs how long the first comparison took when review starts. ## Styling The elements render into the page (no shadow DOM), so your site's styles apply to them, and they're themed with CSS custom properties such as `--ascribe-tip-color` and `--ascribe-tab-active-color`. The [element library's README](https://github.com/ascribed-dev/ascribe/blob/main/packages/elements/README.md#theming) lists them, and shows how to style your own note types and lifecycle states. Their names don't change, but their default colors are Ascribe's and may change in a release, as the changelog notes, so set the ones your site needs fixed. ### Code block titles Available: Ascribe (GA, 0.2.0+) A code block's title, such as a [`@snippet`](https://ascribed-dev.com/reference/directives/#snippet)'s `title`, is in its info string (` ```mjs title="astro.config.mjs" `). Astro's highlighting ignores it, so the integration adds a Shiki transformer that puts a titled block in a figure with the title as its caption: ```html <figure class="code-title"> <figcaption>astro.config.mjs</figcaption> <pre class="astro-code">…</pre> </figure> ``` The figure has your browser's default margins, and the caption no style of its own; style `figure.code-title` and its `figcaption` to suit your site. Titles need Astro's default highlighting, Shiki; with `syntaxHighlight: "prism"` or `false`, they aren't shown. ## Other Markdown processors The integration supports Astro's default processor (Sätteri) and `unified()`. Any other processor is an error at startup, since heading ids and image attributes would be lost.

---
title: Make a cup of tea
---

A good cup of tea takes about five minutes, and needs only fresh water, tea, and a little attention to temperature and time.

@note {type=tip}: Use fresh water each time. Water that's been boiled more than once makes tea taste flat.

## What you need

- A kettle
- A mug or a teapot
- Tea: one tea bag, or one teaspoon of loose leaves, for each cup
- Milk, lemon, or honey, if you like them

## Heat the water and steep

The water's temperature and the steeping time depend on the tea:

@variant {tea=black}:
Use water that has just boiled, at 100 °C, and steep for 3 to 5 minutes.
@variant {tea=green}:
Let the boiled water cool for two minutes, to about 80 °C, and steep for 2 to 3 minutes. Hotter water makes green tea bitter.
@variant {tea=herbal}:
Use water that has just boiled, at 100 °C, and steep for 5 to 7 minutes.
@end

## Make the tea

@steps
1. Fill the kettle with fresh water, and heat it.
2. Warm the mug or teapot with a splash of hot water, then pour it away.
3. Add the tea.
4. Pour the water over the tea, and start a timer.
5. When the time is up, take out the tea bag or strain the leaves.
6. Add milk, lemon, or honey to taste.

@note: Don't squeeze the tea bag. It releases tannins that make the tea bitter.
EOF
